blocks.text: Listing resources tells a client what exists. Reading a resource is the step where a client actually gets its content, the text of a file, the rows of a report, the bytes of an image.
That single step, resources/read, is where a URI turns into real content a model can use.
This lesson walks through the request and response shape, the difference between text and binary content, reading one resource versus several, and what a client does once the content finally arrives.
1. What Happens When You Read a Resource

blocks.alt: What Happens When You Read a Resource
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440585339-133054684.png
Reading a resource means asking a server for the actual content behind a URI it already told you about, through resources/list, resources/templates/list, or plain prior knowledge.
The client sends one method call, resources/read, naming the exact URI it wants, and the server responds with the content of that one resource.
Nothing about listing or discovery happens again here, by the time a client calls resources/read it already knows which URI it wants and is simply asking for the payload.
2. The resources/read Request
A resources/read request is small on purpose, it carries exactly one field that matters, the uri of the resource being requested.
That uri has to be one the server actually recognizes, either a concrete resource it listed or a URI a client built by filling in a template it advertised.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: resources/read takes a single uri, not a list of them. Reading several resources means sending several requests, one per URI.

blocks.text: 3. The resources/read Response Shape
The response wraps everything in a contents array, even when there is only one item inside it.
Each entry in contents repeats the uri it belongs to, carries a mimeType describing the kind of content, and then either a text field or a blob field holding the actual payload.

blocks.title: Why an array
blocks.content: A single URI can sometimes expand into more than one content entry, for example a resource that bundles both a rendered view and raw source. Most of the time you will see exactly one entry.

blocks.text: 4. Text Content
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440585339-677579536.png
When a resource holds readable text, source code, markdown, plain logs, JSON configuration, the server puts that text directly in the text field as a plain string.
No encoding step is needed here, the string a client reads out of text is exactly the content it would see opening that file in a text editor.
5. Binary Content and the blob Field
Images, PDFs, audio clips, and any other content that is not plain text arrives in the blob field instead, as a base64 encoded string.
A client has to base64 decode that string before the bytes are usable, whether that means writing them to disk, rendering an image, or passing them along to something else.

blocks.text: 6. The mimeType Field
mimeType is what tells a client which of the two fields to expect and how to treat the content once it arrives.
A client should trust mimeType over guessing from the file extension in the URI, since the server is the one that actually knows what it is serving.

blocks.text: 7. Reading One Resource by URI
The simplest and most common case is a client that already knows exactly one URI it wants and calls resources/read once.
This is the pattern behind most everyday reads, a user or model picks one file, one row, one document, and the client fetches exactly that.
8. Reading Multiple Resources at Once
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440585339-946976005.png
There is no batch version of resources/read that accepts a list of URIs in one call, each read is still one request for one URI.
What a client can do instead is issue several resources/read calls concurrently, when it already knows it wants several distinct resources at the same time.

code.content:
import asyncio

async def read_many(session, uris):
    tasks = [session.read_resource(uri) for uri in uris]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    return dict(zip(uris, results))

uris = [
    "file:///project/README.md",
    "file:///project/package.json",
    "file:///project/src/app.py"
]
contents = await read_many(session, uris)

items: One resources/read request always names exactly one uri.
A single response can still contain more than one entry in contents, for a resource that expands into several pieces.
Fetching several distinct resources means firing several requests, sequentially or concurrently, from the client side.

blocks.text: 9. How a Client Uses Content Once It Arrives
Getting the contents array back is only the halfway point, the client still has real work to do with it.

items: Check whether each entry has text or blob and branch accordingly.
Decode any blob content from base64 before it is usable as raw bytes.
Decide how much of a large text resource actually belongs in the current context.
Format the content into whatever shape the next step expects, a chat message, a file write, a rendered preview.

blocks.text: 10. Injecting Resource Content Into an LLM Context

blocks.alt: Injecting Resource Content Into an LLM Context
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586019-795859048.png
The most common destination for resource content, in an AI assisted client, is the model context itself, as another message the model can read.
A client typically wraps the raw text in a small amount of framing so the model knows where it came from.
Binary content is rarely pasted into a text context directly, most clients either describe it, as shown above, or hand it to a separate step built for images or files.
A large text resource may also need trimming or summarizing before it goes into context, since context windows are finite and a whole file might not fit.
11. Error Case: Resource Not Found
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586019-159740456.png
If the uri in a resources/read request does not match anything the server knows about, the server returns an error instead of a contents array.
A well behaved client treats this as a normal, expected outcome, not a crash, since resources can be renamed, deleted, or simply mistyped.
12. Error Case: Permission Denied
A URI can be perfectly valid and still be off limits to the caller asking for it, a private record, a restricted file, a resource tied to another user.

blocks.title: Do not leak details
blocks.content: A good permission denied error explains that access was refused without revealing whether the record even exists, so a client cannot use error responses to probe for data it should never see.

blocks.text: 13. Other Errors and Edge Cases
Not found and permission denied are the two you will hit most, but a few other failure shapes are worth recognizing too.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Error case","Typical code","What it means"],"rows":[["Resource not found","-32002 or a custom code","The uri does not match any resource the server knows about"],["Permission denied","-32001 or a custom code","The caller is not allowed to read this resource"],["Invalid uri","-32602 Invalid params","The uri is malformed, missing, or the wrong shape entirely"],["Internal error","-32603 Internal error","Something failed while the server was reading the underlying content"]]}

blocks.text: A client that treats every error the same, as a generic failure, misses a chance to react sensibly, retrying a transient internal error is reasonable, retrying a permission denial is not.
14. Caching Considerations
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586019-699703254.png
Reading the same resource over and over, especially a large file, wastes both time and tokens if nothing about it has actually changed.
A client can keep a small local cache, keyed by uri, and reuse a recent read instead of calling resources/read again right away.

blocks.title: Cache the right thing
blocks.content: Cache the contents you got back for a uri, not whether the read succeeded at all. A cached error can hide a resource that has since become readable again.

blocks.text: 15. Cache Invalidation and Staleness
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586020-858898670.png
The hard part of caching is never storing the value, it is knowing when that stored value is no longer true.
A resource behind a URI can change between reads, a file gets edited, a database row gets updated, a search result set shifts.

items: Use a short time to live for resources that change often, and a longer one for resources that rarely do.
Drop a cached entry the moment a related tool call or notification suggests the underlying data changed.
Prefer a fresh read over a stale cached one whenever correctness matters more than speed.
Never cache a resource read forever with no expiry at all, that just guarantees staleness eventually.

blocks.text: Worked Example
Picture an MCP server for an internal wiki. A client already has the uri wiki://engineering/onboarding-guide, learned from an earlier resources/list call.
The server responds with the page as markdown text, tagged with the right mimeType.

The client checks the cache first, finds nothing recent enough, calls resources/read, then wraps the returned text in a message and appends it to the conversation before the model answers a question about onboarding.
It also stores the result in its cache, keyed by that uri, so a second question about the same page a minute later does not trigger another round trip.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming resources/read accepts an array of URIs in one call, it does not, one request reads one uri.
Ignoring mimeType and guessing content type from the file extension in the URI instead.
Pasting raw base64 blob content straight into an LLM context as if it were readable text.
Treating every read error the same way instead of reacting differently to not found, permission denied, and internal error.
Caching forever with no expiry, so a client keeps serving content that changed hours or days ago.
Caching a failed read and refusing to try again even after the underlying resource became available.

blocks.text: Practice
A server exposes billing://invoices/9931 as a JSON invoice resource. Write the resources/read request for it, and sketch the response you would expect back, including a sensible mimeType.
Key Takeaway
resources/read turns a known uri into real content, a text field or a blob field, tagged with a mimeType that says how to treat it.

A client checks that mimeType, decodes binary content when needed, shapes text content for the model context, reacts sensibly to not found and permission denied errors, and caches results carefully so it is not re-reading unchanged content on every turn.
